title: aienai.co
summary: AIENAI's corporate site, with motion-led interactions and Vercel edge functions.
body:
AIENAI's corporate site at www.aienai.co: motion-led interactions on the front end, Vercel edge functions behind it. React and TypeScript on Vite. 38 of 49 commits are mine.

## Motion as argument

A consultancy site has one job: convince a visitor that the people behind it can actually do the thing. For a firm selling design and engineering, the site is the sample. Motion that is smooth, purposeful and not gratuitous is a more credible claim than any case study on the page, because it demonstrates rather than asserts.

The discipline is knowing when to stop. Motion that draws attention to itself has switched from evidence to decoration.

## Edge functions for the parts that cannot be static

Most of a corporate site should be static and fast. The exceptions are the bits that need to run per request, and putting those at the edge rather than in a server keeps the whole thing on one deployment with no origin to maintain.

## Building for your own employer is its own constraint

There is no client to arbitrate. Everyone has an opinion and everyone can reach you. Internal work tends to accumulate revisions in a way client work does not, because nothing forces a decision to be final. The counterweight is that you can ship a change the same afternoon somebody notices a problem.

## The apex domain is a known issue

The site lives at www.aienai.co. The apex does not resolve, which is a DNS matter rather than a build one, but it is worth stating here rather than letting someone discover it by typing the shorter address.

title: Fresh Pick Mart
summary: Retail brand identity: logo, packaging, signage and in-store graphics with a style guide.
body:
Retail brand identity for FreshPick: logo, packaging, signage and in-store graphics, delivered with a brand style guide. Brand identity designer, 2021.

## Retail is where identity gets tested in three dimensions

Most brand work lives on screens and in documents. Retail does not. The same mark has to work on a shelf-edge label two inches wide, on a shopfront sign read from across a road, and on packaging a customer picks up and turns over in their hand. Those are three different viewing distances, three different materials and three different lighting conditions, and a system that only solves one of them is not finished.

## Packaging is a legibility problem with a legal component

There is a fixed amount of surface, a mandatory set of information that has to appear on it, and a customer making a decision in a few seconds while holding something else in the other hand. The design freedom is whatever is left after the required elements are placed, which is far less than a blank comp suggests.

## The style guide is the actual deliverable

A logo handed over on its own has a short life. The guide is what lets a shop owner, a printer and whoever does the next campaign produce material that still looks like the same business in a year, once the designer is no longer in the room.

## Early work, deliberately kept

This is from 2021 and it is earlier than most of what is on this site. It stays because packaging and signage demonstrate range that screen work cannot, and because a portfolio that quietly deletes everything before a certain date is telling you less than it thinks.

title: AMMBAN
summary: Complete visual identity system and 200+ marketing assets for a national mobile-money agents association.
body:
A complete visual identity system for AMMBAN, the Association of Mobile Money and Bank Agents of Nigeria, plus over 200 marketing assets built on it: logo suite, event branding, certificates, social templates and brand guidelines. Lead brand designer, 2024 to present.

## Two hundred assets is a systems problem, not a logo project

Once the volume passes a certain point the mark stops being the deliverable and the rules become the deliverable. Nobody can hand-make two hundred pieces and keep them coherent, and nobody should try. What has to exist instead is a set of decisions specific enough that someone else can make the two hundred and first piece correctly without asking.

## Who the association actually serves

AMMBAN represents mobile money and bank agents: the people running point-of-sale terminals in markets, shopfronts and roadside kiosks across the country. That audience changes the identity brief in a concrete way. Assets are seen printed cheaply, at small sizes, in bright sun, on materials nobody specified, and often reproduced by a local printer working from a screenshot.

An identity that only survives in a controlled environment is not an identity for this organisation. The mark has to hold up in one colour, at low resolution, badly cropped.

## Certificates and event branding carry more weight than they look

For a membership association, a certificate is not a decorative artefact. It is the thing a member puts on the wall of a kiosk as proof of legitimacy to a customer deciding whether to hand over cash. Event branding does the same job at scale for the organisation itself. Both are trust instruments, which is a higher bar than looking good.

## Campaign creative on top of the system

The same system carries campaign work supporting membership growth and event attendance, which is the real test: a set of rules built only for identity pieces usually breaks the first time somebody needs a promotional layout with too much copy and a deadline.

title: Xafe
summary: Personal finance mobile application built in Flutter.
body:
A personal finance mobile application built in Flutter. Sole author across two repositories, the original and a later iteration under the CRCT3 organisation.

## Finance apps fail on trust, not on features

Any app that shows someone their money is asking for a level of confidence that a to-do list never has to earn. That shapes everything: what is displayed while data is loading, how a failed sync is communicated, and whether a number on screen is ever allowed to be stale without saying so.

The temptation with a personal project is to fake all of that with placeholder data and call it done. The interesting version is the one that behaves correctly when the network is not there.

## Flutter for a single-developer mobile product

One codebase, two platforms, and a widget model that makes a custom interface cheaper than the native equivalents. For an individual building a finance app with an opinionated look, that trade is the right one, and it is the same reasoning that later applied to OutOut at much larger scale.

## Honest scope

A personal project, not a shipped product with users. It is here as early evidence of Flutter work and of a particular care about how financial information is presented, both of which turn up again later in this portfolio at a much bigger size.

title: Hikima Academy
summary: Education marketing site with a custom CMS and course-enrolment flow.
body:
An education marketing site with a custom CMS and a course-enrolment flow for Hikima Academy, a cybersecurity and IT education provider. Designer and developer, built in Framer.

## A course catalogue is an information architecture problem

Hikima's offering spans foundational tracks (network administration, information security, software engineering, data science, forensics, cloud, identity and access management) and advanced specialisms on top of them. A prospective learner arrives knowing roughly what they want to become and nothing about how the tracks relate.

Presenting that as a flat list of courses fails everyone. The structure has to answer "where do I start" and "what does this lead to" before it answers "what is in module three".

## Cybersecurity education has a specific credibility problem

The field is full of providers promising employment outcomes. A marketing site for one of them is read sceptically by default, which means concrete specifics (named domains, hands-on labs, what a placement actually involves) do more work than any amount of confident copy.

## A custom CMS because the catalogue changes

Course content in this field goes stale fast. The CMS exists so the team can add a track, retire one, or change a module list without a developer in the loop. That is the difference between a site that is current in eighteen months and one that quietly becomes a liability.

[YEMI: the live site at hikimaacademy.net no longer looks like a Framer build, so it may have been rebuilt since. Worth checking whether the link should still point there, and whether this should be described in the past tense.]

title: All Saints University
summary: University admission and document-management portal, built during the Hikima Academy engagement.
body:
A university admission and document-management web application, built during my Hikima Academy engagement. Design plus a small number of commits: 2 of 22 in the repository, alongside David Yusuf and others.

## The credit, stated first

I was not the lead engineer on this. Two commits is two commits, and I am not going to present a supporting contribution as ownership. My contribution was design and a hand in the build.

## Admissions is a document problem wearing an application's clothes

The visible product is a form. The actual product is everything behind it: transcripts, identity documents, references and certificates arriving in every format a scanner or a phone camera can produce, each needing to be attached to the right applicant, checked by a human, and retrievable months later when somebody queries a decision.

Design a portal around the form and you build something that collapses the first week it is used. Design it around the document lifecycle and the form becomes the easy part.

## Applicants are one-time users under stress

Nobody applies to university often enough to learn an interface, and they are doing it at a moment that matters. That rules out anything requiring familiarity: no hidden state, no multi-session flows that lose work, no error messages that assume the reader knows what a field is for.

## Why it is listed

Because it is real, it shipped, and it is the kind of unglamorous institutional software that most portfolios omit in favour of prettier things.

title: 7th Infotech LMS
summary: Learning management system for 7th Infotech: information architecture, user flows and UI, at WCAG 2.1 AA.
body:
The learning management system built at 7th Infotech, where I was UX/UI and brand designer. I designed the information architecture, the user flows and the interface. I did not write the code: the repositories are authored by the engineering team.

## Information architecture is the whole job in an LMS

A learning platform has courses, modules, lessons, cohorts, assessments, progress and roles, and every one of those has a relationship to the others. Get the model wrong and no amount of interface work rescues it, because the navigation will be describing a structure that does not match how anyone teaches or learns.

The work was mostly upstream of any screen: deciding what contains what, what a learner sees versus an instructor versus an administrator, and where progress actually lives.

## WCAG 2.1 AA as a starting constraint, not an audit

Applied during design rather than checked afterwards. That ordering is the difference between accessibility being a set of colour and focus decisions made once, and being a retrofit that fights every layout it touches. Contrast ratios, target sizes, focus order and non-colour status indicators are all cheaper to decide at wireframe stage than to repair.

## Design without the build is still design

This is one of the entries on this site where I was not the engineer, and saying so is more useful than blurring it. The portfolio is stronger for containing both kinds of work, clearly labelled.

title: LeanHQ
summary: Internal ops platform and Nigerian-first HRIS.
body:
LeanHQ is an internal operations platform and a Nigerian-first HRIS, built on Next.js 15, React 19 and Supabase. Supporting contributor.

## Nigerian-first is the whole product

Most HRIS products are built for a US or European payroll reality and then localised badly: tax logic that does not match, leave types that do not exist here, salary structures that assume monthly PAYE in a currency that is not the one anyone is paid in. Building it Nigerian-first instead of localising afterwards is a different product decision, not a translation exercise.

## What I contributed

Interface patterns kept in step with the shared design language across the AIENAI portfolio, and delivery support. I did not lead this one and there are no commits of mine in the repository, so the credit here is supporting contributor and nothing more.

## Why internal tools are worth listing

An ops platform has no marketing budget, no onboarding funnel and no forgiving first-time user. The people using it are colleagues who will tell you immediately and directly when a flow wastes their afternoon. That feedback loop is faster and more honest than anything a consumer product gets.

title: Settle In
summary: Relocation product in the AIENAI portfolio.
body:
Settle In is a relocation product in the AIENAI portfolio, built on Next.js. Supporting contributor.

## The scope, stated plainly

I supported delivery and kept interface patterns consistent with the shared design language. I did not lead it and I have no commits in the repository. Supporting contributor is the accurate credit and it is the one I will use.

## Relocation is a trust problem before it is a software problem

Someone moving country is making the highest-stakes set of decisions they will make in a decade, usually with incomplete information, often in a second language, and frequently after being let down by an agent or a landlord. The interface work is not about efficiency. It is about making a process legible enough that a person can tell whether they are being treated fairly.

## Why the small ones are still listed

Thirty-four projects on this site, and not all of them are headline work. A portfolio that shows only the highlights is a highlight reel, and a highlight reel tells you nothing about how someone works on the ordinary days, which is most days.

title: eventX
summary: Event management app: organisers host events, visitors browse and reserve. Vue, still deployed.
body:
An event management application: organisers host events, visitors browse them and make reservations. Built in Vue and still deployed at event-x-pink.vercel.app. 25 commits, sole author, with a second 25-commit rebuild in 2024.

## Early work, and why it is still here

This is 2022, which makes it the oldest thing on this site by some distance. It stays for one reason: it is a complete two-sided product built alone. An organiser side that creates and manages events, and a visitor side that finds and books them, are two different products sharing a database, and getting both coherent is a harder first project than most people attempt.

## Two-sided means two different definitions of done

The organiser needs control: capacity, timing, changes after publication. The visitor needs certainty: is this still on, did my reservation register, what happens if it is cancelled. Those pull in opposite directions, and the reservation flow is where they meet. Almost every failure mode in event software is a state that one side thinks it changed and the other has not seen.

## Vue, deliberately

Vue rather than React, which is worth stating in a portfolio that otherwise runs on React. The framework was the right size for the problem at the time and I still list Vue as something I work in rather than something I once touched.

## Rebuilt in 2024

A second pass under a separate repository, same idea, better structure. Keeping both is honest about how the work actually went: the first version taught me what the second one needed to be.

title: Devign Figma MCP
summary: AI-to-Figma Model Context Protocol server exposing 40 design tools over WebSocket.
body:
A Model Context Protocol server that gives an AI assistant hands inside Figma: 40 design tools exposed over WebSocket, so a model can create, inspect and modify a document rather than only describe one. Open source at github.com/sodiqogundairo/devign-figma-mcp.

## The interesting half of AI in design is the doing, not the describing

Every AI design tool that generates an image is solving the easy half. The hard half is acting on a real document: reading the layer tree, respecting components, writing changes back in a form a designer can then edit by hand. A model that produces a picture of a screen has produced nothing you can ship. A model that can restructure an auto-layout frame has.

## Forty tools, and why the number matters

Forty is roughly the surface you need before an assistant stops being a demo. Create, read, update and delete across frames, text, components, styles and variables, because a model that can create but not inspect will confidently overwrite work, and one that can inspect but not modify is a search engine.

## WebSocket, not REST

Figma's plugin sandbox and an external model do not share a process, so the transport has to be persistent and bidirectional: the model asks, the plugin answers from inside the document, and both stay connected across a long editing session. REST would mean re-establishing context on every call, which is the thing that makes AI tooling feel slow and stupid.

## It is the other half of Devign

Devign is the component library; this is the bridge that lets a model work with it. Together they are an attempt at the same idea from both ends: design decisions captured as code, reachable by a person or by a machine.

title: YAHWCF
summary: Site for the Yoruba Annual World Heritage Cultural Festival.
body:
A site for the Yoruba Annual World Heritage Cultural Festival. Designer and developer, built with Tailwind CSS and JavaScript.

## Cultural work has a different failure mode

Design for a heritage festival can go wrong in two opposite directions: sanitising the subject into something generic and corporate, or reaching for decorative pastiche that reduces a living culture to a pattern. Both are disrespectful and both are common.

The useful position is restraint with specificity. Let the photography, the names and the programme carry the cultural weight, and keep the interface quiet enough not to editorialise over them.

## A festival site is a deadline with a date attached

Everything has to be right before the event, and after the event most of the traffic stops. That shapes the priorities: programme, dates, location and how to attend come first, and anything that cannot be finished in time should not be started.

## Scope, stated plainly

Designer and developer on a contained site. This is a brief, not a long case study, which is the honest length for it.

title: SUAP
summary: Front-end web app for a crypto company.
body:
A front-end web application for a crypto company. Front-end developer, not designer or lead. React and Tailwind CSS.

## Crypto front ends have a specific, unforgiving problem

The numbers move, the numbers are money, and users act on them immediately. A stale price is not a cosmetic bug, it is a user making a decision on information that is no longer true. That single fact drives most of the engineering: how often to update, what to show while updating, and what to do when the connection to the source is lost.

The wrong answer is showing a plausible old number with no indication it is old. The right answer is usually visible degradation, which designers tend to resist because it looks broken. It is meant to.

## Precision is not a display preference

Floating point is the wrong type for money and very much the wrong type for assets quoted to eight decimal places. Rounding for display has to happen at the last possible moment and never in the value that gets submitted. This is a solved problem that gets re-broken constantly.

## The honest scope

I was a front-end developer on this, not the designer and not the lead. The credit here is implementation.

title: Ladire
summary: Storefront and brand-aligned shopping experience for a Nigerian Adire textile business.
body:
A storefront and brand-aligned shopping experience for Ladire by Lade, a Nigerian Adire textile business. Designer and developer, on Shopify.

## The domain has lapsed

ladirebylade.com no longer resolves to the shop; it now redirects to a domain-parking page. The link has been removed from this page rather than left to send visitors somewhere misleading. The work happened and is described honestly here, but I am not going to point at something that is no longer there.

## Adire is a craft product, which changes the storefront problem

Adire is hand-dyed indigo textile with a visible making process and genuine variation between pieces. That breaks the default e-commerce assumption that a product photo represents an identical unit in a warehouse. The design job is to make variation read as provenance rather than as inconsistency, which is mostly about photography direction, how a product page frames the maker, and being explicit about what will differ.

## Brand-aligned means the theme is not the brand

A Shopify theme gives you a working shop in an afternoon and a shop that looks like every other shop by the evening. The work is in the parts a theme does not have opinions about: how the collection is organised, what the product page leads with, and whether the whole thing feels like the business or like the platform.

## Shopify was the right call

For a small textile business, a custom build would have meant ongoing maintenance nobody was going to fund. Shopify handles payments, inventory and shipping, and the effort goes into the parts that are actually differentiated. Choosing the boring platform is frequently the correct design decision.

title: ECOSYSTEM
summary: Redesign of the organisation's official site.
body:
A redesign of an organisation's official site. Designer and developer, React and Tailwind CSS.

## Redesign is a different job to design

There is an existing site, existing content, existing URLs and existing expectations from people who already use it. The work starts with an audit rather than a blank page: what does the current site do well, what is actually broken, and which of the complaints are about the site versus about the organisation.

The most common failure in a redesign is solving the aesthetic problem while leaving the structural one untouched, so the new site looks better and is equally hard to use in six months.

## Keeping what works is a decision, not laziness

A redesign that changes everything forces every existing user to relearn the site, and spends goodwill on things they never complained about. Deciding what to leave alone is as deliberate as deciding what to change.

## Scope

Designer and developer. A brief rather than an extended case study, which is the right length for the work.

title: DevignFX
summary: Multi-strategy algorithmic trading bot that auto-discovers every instrument a broker offers, with copy trading.
body:
A multi-strategy algorithmic trading bot for MetaTrader 5, written in Python. It auto-discovers every instrument a given broker offers rather than being configured per symbol, and supports copy trading. 83 commits, sole author.

## Auto-discovery is the part worth explaining

Almost every retail trading bot is configured symbol by symbol: you tell it to trade EURUSD, you tell it the tick size, you tell it the session hours. That is fine until the broker changes its instrument list, renames a symbol, or you move brokers entirely, at which point the configuration is silently wrong and the bot keeps trading anyway.

This one interrogates the broker instead. It reads the full instrument list at runtime, around 350 on the broker it was built against, and derives contract size, tick value and session from the terminal rather than from a file somebody maintained six months ago.

## Multi-strategy means the risk question gets harder

One strategy on one symbol has a simple position-sizing answer. Several strategies across hundreds of instruments can quietly build a correlated position that looks diversified and is not: twelve separate longs on twelve pairs that all share a dollar leg is one trade, not twelve.

## Copy trading changes who is exposed

The moment another account mirrors yours, a bug stops being your loss and becomes someone else's. That is a different standard of care than a personal script, and it is the reason this one is conservative about what it will act on automatically.

## The honest limit

This is a personal system, not a product with users or a track record I am publishing. It is on this page as evidence of a particular kind of engineering (live market data, broker APIs, state that must survive a disconnect mid-position) rather than as a claim about returns.

title: Moniepoint, South West
summary: Regional visual identity system and campaign creative supporting sales and recruitment.
body:
Regional visual identity and campaign creative for Moniepoint in the South West of Nigeria, supporting sales, recruitment and brand awareness. Brand and identity designer, contract, December 2023 to present.

## Working inside someone else's brand is a different discipline

Moniepoint is a large, established fintech with an existing identity, and this is regional work sitting underneath it. That inverts the usual brand brief. There is no blank page and no opportunity to be clever with the mark. The job is to produce material that is unmistakably Moniepoint while doing something the national brand system was never designed to do.

## What a region actually needs that head office does not supply

Recruitment drives for agents, sales material aimed at a specific market, campaign creative tied to local events and local language. Central brand teams build for the national case and ship a guideline document. The regional case is where that document either holds or turns out to have never anticipated a Saturday recruitment push in a specific town.

## The constraint is restraint

The measure of this kind of work is that nobody notices it. If a regional asset reads as a different company, or as an off-brand knock-off of the real thing, it has failed regardless of how good the layout is. Getting that right is mostly about knowing which parts of a system are load-bearing and which have flex in them.

## Why it is listed as contract

It is contract work alongside a full-time role, and saying so is more useful than implying I ran brand at a company of that size. The credit is brand and identity designer for one region.

title: Microsoft AgroTech Hackathon
summary: Event identity: logo, participant badges, certificates, stage backdrops and a social campaign package.
body:
Event identity for the Microsoft AgroTech Hackathon: logo, participant badges, certificates, stage backdrops and a social campaign asset package. Brand and visual designer, 2022.

## An event has a deadline that does not move

The date is the date. There is no scope negotiation on the morning of, no shipping a fix next sprint, and every asset has to be finished, printed and physically present. That single constraint governs the whole process and makes event work a useful discipline for anyone who mostly builds software, where deadlines are usually softer than anyone admits.

## Scale changes the design, not just the export settings

A stage backdrop is printed at a size where a decision that looked fine at 100 percent zoom becomes a visible flaw across several metres. Line weights, kerning and image resolution all have to be considered at final size rather than on screen. A badge has the opposite problem: it is small, it is read at arm's length, and it has to carry a name legibly while still reading as part of the same family as the backdrop behind it.

## Certificates and badges do participant-facing work

They are the two pieces every attendee physically holds and keeps. The badge is worn for the duration and is how people identify each other; the certificate is the artefact that outlives the event and gets photographed and posted. For a hackathon, those two items do more brand work than anything else produced.

## The social package is the reach

The event has a few hundred people in a room. The campaign asset package is what carries it to everyone who was not there, and it has to be built so organisers can deploy it themselves during the event rather than waiting on a designer.

title: Brand Applied
summary: Identity systems taken off the page and onto real things: apparel, merchandise, uniform.
body:
Identity systems taken off the page and onto real things: apparel, merchandise and uniform. Brand designer.

## Applied is where identity either survives or falls apart

A mark that reads perfectly on a screen can disappear when it is embroidered, stretched across a shoulder seam, printed on a curved surface, or reproduced in a single thread colour by a supplier who has never seen the guidelines. Application is the stress test, and a surprising amount of otherwise good identity work fails it.

## Embroidery removes the things you were relying on

Fine lines fill in. Gradients are not available. Small text turns into texture. Anything below a certain stroke weight simply does not exist once it is thread. A system that has not planned for this ends up with a special one-off version of the logo for shirts, which is the precise moment a brand starts fragmenting.

The fix is upstream: design a mark that already has a reduced form, and specify it, rather than improvising one under deadline pressure at a supplier.

## Uniform is the hardest case

It is worn by people who did not choose it, in front of customers, all day. It has to survive washing, it has to work across body shapes and garment colours, and it has to be something staff are not embarrassed to be seen in. That last requirement is a design constraint even though it never appears in a brief.

## Why this is one entry rather than several

These are pieces of applied work across different clients rather than a single engagement, grouped because what they demonstrate is the same thing: what happens to identity after handover.

title: Print & Editorial
summary: Book covers, stationery and event print, from cover art through to finished mockups.
body:
Book covers, stationery and event print: cover art through to finished mockups. Designer.

## Print does not forgive

A screen is a forgiving medium. It is backlit, it is a known size, the colour space is predictable, and a mistake is a redeploy away from being fixed. Print is none of those things. Ink behaves differently on different stock, a colour that sang on a monitor can go muddy on uncoated paper, and a misjudged margin becomes ten thousand copies of a misjudged margin.

Designing for it teaches a kind of care that transfers directly to everything else. If you have had to specify bleed and trim on something irreversible, you stop being casual about spacing on a screen.

## A book cover is a single-frame argument

It has one job, performed at thumbnail size in a list, in a fraction of a second, against competitors doing the same thing. There is no scroll, no second screen, no progressive disclosure. Every decision about type weight, image crop and contrast is made against that one exposure.

It is the purest exercise in hierarchy available, and it is why cover work is worth keeping in a portfolio that is otherwise about software.

## Mockups are part of the deliverable, not decoration

Taking cover art through to a finished mockup is what lets a client see the object rather than the file. A flat JPEG asks someone to imagine a physical thing; a mockup removes the imagination step, and the number of revision rounds usually drops because of it.

title: TedPrime Hub
summary: Company site and hub.
body:
A company site and content hub for TEDPRIME, where I worked as a product designer and front-end developer. Designer and developer, built in HTML, CSS and JavaScript.

## A content hub is a maintenance problem before it is a design problem

Anything that publishes regularly will be judged on its twentieth article, not its first. The structure has to work when there are a hundred pieces and several categories, and it has to be editable by whoever is actually writing rather than by the person who built it.

## Hand-built, and why that was right at the time

HTML, CSS and JavaScript rather than a framework. For a site of this size and at that point, a build step and a dependency tree would have been overhead with no return, and plain files are still the most maintainable thing you can hand to a team that does not have a front-end engineer.

That is worth stating in a portfolio that otherwise leans heavily on React: choosing the smaller tool when it fits is the same skill as choosing the larger one when it does not.

## Context

This sits alongside the TEDPRIME role in my experience, where the larger piece of work was establishing the company's first component-based design system across web and mobile. This site was the public-facing part of that period.

title: Fountium
summary: Corporate marketing site.
body:
A corporate marketing site for Fountium. Designer and developer, React and Tailwind CSS.

## A corporate site is a qualification tool

The visitor is deciding in about fifteen seconds whether this company is plausibly the sort of organisation they need. That decision is made on register and clarity long before anyone reads a service description. The design work is mostly about removing the things that erode credibility: vague copy, stock imagery, a navigation that hides what the business actually does.

## Built rather than themed

React and Tailwind rather than a page builder, which is a deliberate trade. More effort up front, and in return the layout is not fighting a theme's assumptions and the page weight stays low enough to load properly on a slow connection, which is the condition a large share of the audience is actually on.

## Small site, same discipline

This is a brief rather than a long case study, because it was a contained piece of work and inflating it would be dishonest. The parts worth stating are the ones above: what the site has to achieve in the first fifteen seconds, and why it was built rather than assembled.

title: Flock ChMS
summary: Eighteen admin modules, twenty member surfaces and a platform console, designed and built end to end.
body:
Flock is a multi-tenant church platform. Eighteen admin modules, twenty member-facing surfaces, three separate audiences and a platform console of its own, sitting on 63 Supabase edge functions and 554 migrations. 664 commits, all of them mine.

[YEMI: this needs its origin in your words. Was there a specific church, a conversation, a thing you watched somebody do badly in a spreadsheet? Everything below is verifiable from the code. This paragraph is the part only you can write, and it is the part a reader will remember.]

## Fourteen was the wrong number

My own copy has been saying fourteen modules. On the admin side alone it is eighteen: analytics, attendance, billing, communications, community, dashboard, discipleship, engagement, finance, forms, media, members, pastoral care, programs, reports, settings, testimonies and users.

The count matters, but not as a boast. Eighteen is roughly the point at which a product either becomes a platform or quietly becomes eighteen small applications wearing the same logo. Everything interesting about this build was refusing the second outcome.

## Tenancy is resolved once, and nothing below it gets a vote

The failure mode in multi-tenant software is that each module grows its own opinion: its own idea of who the current user is, its own permission checks, its own notion of what a term or a campus or a service is. It works for the first three modules and becomes unmaintainable by the tenth.

So tenancy, auth and the interface primitives live in internal packages rather than in the modules that consume them:

- `packages/tenant` resolves which church you are in, once
- `packages/auth` owns identity and role, and every module reads the same permission set
- `packages/ui` means no module ships its own button

A module cannot answer "which church is this" for itself, because it has no way to ask. That constraint is the architecture.

## Three audiences, one codebase

Admin, member and guest are genuinely different products with different risk profiles. An admin deletes people. A member sees only themselves. A guest is not authenticated at all. They are separate route trees over shared packages rather than one interface with things hidden, because hiding is not a security model.

Above all of them is a platform console: plans, platform roles, subscription retry and cancellation. That is the part that makes it a business rather than an installation.

## The work is mostly in the edges

63 edge functions is where the real complexity ended up, and looking at the list is a fair summary of what running this actually involves: church signup and slug checking, user creation and deletion, subscription retry and cancellation, email OAuth and secret handling and unsubscribe, event reminder scanning, a daily automation pass, an error digest, a developer API, signed Cloudinary uploads.

Almost none of that is visible in a screenshot. All of it is the difference between a demo and something a church can run on a Sunday.

## What I would do differently

554 migrations for one product is a lot. Honestly read, that number says the schema was discovered rather than designed: I learned what a church actually needed by building it, and the migration history is the record of that learning. It works, and the cost is that nobody can reconstruct the intent of the data model by reading it.

[YEMI: do you agree with that reading? If you do it is a strong thing to say out loud, because it is the kind of judgement people hire a senior for. If you think the migration count has another explanation, say so instead and I will rewrite it.]

Real usage as it stands: 832 members, 4,219 messages, 2,242 attendance records and 1,100 emails sent.

title: AXE LMS
summary: Learning platform for teen learners on the AXE AI and design bootcamp.
body:
AXE LMS is a learning platform for teen learners on the AXE AI and design bootcamp, built on Next.js 16 and Supabase with Sentry for error reporting. I am a supporting contributor, not its lead.

## Why a project I did not lead is on this page

Because the alternative is a portfolio that only shows work where I held the pen, and that is not what most engineering actually looks like. On AXE LMS the job was keeping interface patterns consistent with the shared design language while other people owned the product decisions, which is its own skill and a quieter one.

## What supporting actually meant

Pattern consistency against the design system, and delivery support rather than direction. There are no commits of mine to point at in the repository, so I will not claim lead engineer or lead designer on it. That distinction runs through this whole portfolio: where I built it, it says so and there is a commit count.

## The audience is the interesting constraint

Teenagers are the hardest learners to design an LMS for. They abandon anything that feels like homework software, they are on phones, and they have no professional motivation to push through a bad flow. A platform for adult upskilling can get away with being dry. This one cannot.

title: Devign
summary: Published React component library: 40+ accessible components, design tokens, theming and a setup CLI.
body:
Devign is a React component library on npm: 43 components, design tokens, theming and a setup CLI. Built on Radix for behaviour, Tailwind v4 for styling, Motion for animation. 67 commits, sole author, and it is now the interface layer under my own production work.

[YEMI: why did you build this rather than use shadcn, Radix directly, or Mantine? There is a real answer and it is the whole reason the project exists. Without it a reader assumes you did not know the alternatives.]

## A library earns its keep by being used, not by existing

The test of a component library is not its README. It is whether the person who wrote it reaches for it under deadline, on a real project, when hand-rolling would be faster.

LightLife Church runs on Devign in production. So does this portfolio. That is the only claim about it worth making, and it is the one most component libraries cannot make.

## Behaviour is borrowed, appearance is owned

Every component wraps Radix rather than reimplementing it. Accessible focus management, keyboard interaction, portalling and dismissal are solved problems with brutal edge cases, and the correct move is to take them.

What is left is the part worth owning: tokens, density, motion and the decisions that make forty components look like one product rather than forty. `npx devign init` writes a themeable token file, so consuming it does not mean inheriting my taste.

## The bug I found in it by using it

Dogfooding produced a real defect, and it is worth writing down because it is the kind that never shows up in a test.

`devign/styles.css` is not a small component sheet. It is a complete precompiled Tailwind build, and in it the media-query blocks are emitted before the unprefixed utilities. Imported in the order the README gives, its own `grid-cols-2` therefore lands later in the cascade than its own `sm:grid-cols-4` and silently beats it at every width.

The symptom is a responsive layout that collapses with no error anywhere. The class is in the DOM. The class is in the stylesheet. It simply loses. On this site one grid was correct and the grid directly beside it was not, which is exactly why it hid for so long.

The workaround is to import Devign before Tailwind. The actual fix belongs in the library, in how the stylesheet is emitted, and it is still outstanding.

[YEMI: this is a flaw in your own product, so it is your call whether it goes on the page. My view is that it should. Finding a subtle cascade bug in your own library by dogfooding it, diagnosing it by byte offset, and saying so publicly reads as senior. Hiding it reads as marketing. But it is your library and your call, and if it stays you should fix it upstream first.]

## Where it is

Published as `devign` on npm, documented at devign-ui.vercel.app. It was called `yems-ui` before.

title: UCDA
summary: Use-case design-review platform for designers.
body:
UCDA, a use-case design-review platform for designers. Lead developer and supporting designer. React and Supabase.

## What it was for

A place to put a design decision in front of other designers against the use case it was meant to serve, rather than against taste. Design review in most organisations collapses into opinion because the brief is not in the room. Anchoring the review to a stated use case is a small structural change that makes disagreement productive.

## An honest note on evidence

The project has been wound down. A collaborator moved the repository and I no longer have access to it, so the Supabase project is the only thing I can still point at. I am not going to claim a commit count I cannot show.

That is worth saying out loud rather than quietly omitting the project. Work disappears: clients fold, repositories move, domains lapse. A portfolio that only contains things still standing is a portfolio with a survivorship problem.

## Lead developer, supporting designer

Both credits are deliberate. I led the build; I supported rather than owned the design direction. Splitting those two is the difference between a claim a reference would confirm and one they would quietly correct.

title: JAYE
role: Lead product designer, brand and identity
summary: AI nightlife app: competitive analysis, research, high-fidelity prototypes, brand and product identity.
body:
JAYE is an AI-assisted nightlife app: competitive analysis, research and high-fidelity prototypes, plus the brand and product identity. Lead product designer. Still in progress.

## What the work had to answer

What was the gap, what did the competitive analysis actually find, and what did the prototype do differently as a result. A product that cannot answer those three is a set of screens.

## Nightlife is a recommendation problem with a trust layer

The obvious product is a list of venues ranked by an algorithm. The real problem is that nightlife decisions are social, time-sensitive and reputational: where you go depends on who else is going, what it is like right now rather than in aggregate, and whether the place is somewhere you would actually be comfortable. A recommendation engine that optimises for rating misses all three.

That is where AI earns its place, or does not. Matching intent and context beats ranking by score, and the design question is how much of that reasoning to expose so a user can correct it.

## Brand and product were one job here

I did the identity as well as the product design, which for a nightlife app is not a separable concern. The visual register is doing product work: it sets an expectation about what kind of night the app is for before a single venue is shown, and getting that wrong makes accurate recommendations feel wrong anyway.

## Why the reasoning is on this page

Because it is the part a finished screen hides. The outcome is visible in the product; the reasoning, the alternatives considered and the thing that was rejected are not.

title: Tori
summary: AI meeting recorder for Windows: native capture over Windows Graphics Capture and WASAPI loopback, with transcription proxied through Supabase edge functions.
body:
Tori is a desktop AI meeting recorder. Electron and TypeScript for the application, a native C# layer for capture, ffmpeg for media handling and Supabase behind it, sole author.

[YEMI: is this shipped, in beta, or shelved? Say so at the top. A reader who cannot tell whether they can use it assumes shelved.]

## Why a native capture layer exists at all

Recording a meeting properly means recording what the other people said, and that is system audio, not the microphone. Browsers cannot do it. Electron cannot do it on its own either.

So capture drops to native Windows APIs: Windows Graphics Capture for the screen and WASAPI loopback for the audio the machine is playing. That is the whole reason a C# component sits inside an otherwise TypeScript application, and it is the part of the product that could not be shortcut.

[YEMI: `homebrew-tori` exists as a repo, which implies Mac distribution, but the capture layer is Windows-only. Is Mac supported, planned, or is the tap left over? I have not claimed either way.]

## The audio was the real problem

Raw meeting audio is unusable for transcription: room echo, reverb, a laptop microphone at the wrong end of a table. Transcription quality is bounded by input quality, and no amount of model choice fixes a bad recording.

The path that worked was a local de-echo and dereverb pass before transcription rather than sending raw audio and hoping.

[YEMI: how much did that actually improve transcript accuracy? Even a rough before-and-after on one real recording would turn this from a plausible claim into evidence, and it is the most interesting number in the project.]

## What I would want to know if I were reading this

[YEMI: two things a reader will ask that I cannot answer. First, why build this when Otter, Granola and Fathom exist. Second, whether it records only your side of the call and what you did about consent, because that is a legal question in the UK and it is the first thing a cautious buyer thinks of.]

title: AIENAI Academy
summary: Learning platform with course catalogue, enrolment, payments and transactional email.
body:
AIENAI Academy: a learning platform with a course catalogue, enrolment, payments and transactional email, at aienai.academy. Designer and lead developer. 108 of 111 commits are mine.

## Enrolment and payment are one flow, not two

The temptation is to treat the catalogue as marketing and the checkout as plumbing. It is the same flow. A learner deciding whether a course is for them and a learner entering card details are the same person thirty seconds apart, and the moment the visual and verbal register changes between those two screens, confidence drops and so does completion.

## Transactional email is part of the product

The receipt, the enrolment confirmation and the access details are, for most learners, the first thing they keep. They arrive when the person is least certain they made a good decision. Treating them as system output rather than as designed communication is a missed opportunity that almost every education platform takes.

## Payments in this market are not a single integration

Cards, bank transfer and local rails all have different failure modes and different user expectations about what "paid" means and how long it takes. Designing a confirmation state that is honest across all of them, rather than optimistically telling everyone they are enrolled, is most of the work.

[YEMI: how does this relate to AXE LMS and to the Gr8QM courses? There are three education products in your portfolio and a reader will want to know whether they are the same thing for different audiences or genuinely different products.]

title: Motif
summary: Desktop motion-graphics studio built on a procedural, data-bindable engine with an AI layer that turns a brief into an editable scene.
body:
Motif is a desktop motion-graphics studio, in build rather than shipped. Tauri with a Rust core and a React interface, owned by Gr8QM Technovates. covering planning, specification and the early build.

Calling it in progress is deliberate. It is on this site because the thinking is worth reading, not because it is finished.

## The scope decision is the interesting part

The full idea is large: references and research, design import, generative video, a web tier, collaboration, general vector authoring. Built in that order it never ships.

So v1 is narrowed to one wedge, the data reel. Paste or connect data, get an on-brand animated chart or stat reel, change the data and it restages itself, export. Nothing else until that works.

That narrowing is the only reason there is a buildable product here at all, and it is the decision I would defend hardest.

## Motion graphics, not video editing

The distinction matters and is easy to blur. A video editor arranges footage on a timeline. A motion-graphics tool generates and animates its own content from parameters, which means the primitives are procedural and data-bindable rather than clips.

Getting that right early is the difference between a product that can restage a reel when the numbers change and one where changing a number means redoing the work.

## Desktop first, and why

[YEMI: why Tauri and desktop rather than web, given your stack is React and TypeScript and Rust is the least familiar part of it? There is presumably a real reason (rendering performance, local file access, export pipeline) and it is worth stating, because choosing the harder path needs a justification a reader can accept.]

[YEMI: this page needs one image or a short clip more than it needs more words. A motion product described only in prose is the least convincing form it could take.]

title: OutOut
summary: Offline-first social events app, live on the App Store, with a clean-architecture sync engine.
body:
OutOut is an offline-first social events app, live on the App Store as `com.outout.mobileapp`. Flutter with BLoC, Drift for local persistence, Supabase behind it and FCM for push. 216 of 252 commits are mine.

[YEMI: what is the product actually for, in one sentence a stranger would understand? "Social events app" is a category, not a proposition.]

## Offline-first was the requirement, not a feature

The users are out, on their phones, in venues, on Nigerian mobile data. An app that assumes a connection is an app that fails at exactly the moment it is being used.

So the local database is the source of truth the interface reads from, and sync is a separate concern that reconciles with the server when it can. Drift holds the local state, BLoC keeps the sync engine out of the widget tree, and the interface never waits on the network to render.

## The incident worth writing about

In July a Supabase upsell notice arrived for what is, by any measure, a small app. Roughly 1.6 million requests in a month against a user base of about a hundred people.

The cause was two things compounding, and neither looked wrong in isolation:

- A query passed an unbounded list of ids into an `in()` filter. Past a certain length the URL exceeded what the endpoint would accept and the request failed with a 400.
- A listener refetched on failure. No backoff, no cooldown, no cap.

A failing request that triggers an immediate retry of the same failing request is a loop that runs as fast as the network allows. The fix was to chunk the id list so the URL can never grow unbounded, and to put a backoff on the retry.

The lesson I took from it is that this class of bug is invisible in testing, because with ten rows the URL is short and the query succeeds. It only appears at the data volume where it costs money, and the first signal was a billing email a month later rather than an alert the same day. A cheap daily request-volume check would have caught it in a day.

## Then I measured what a user actually costs

Because the incident made the question concrete, I measured the full cost to serve one monthly active user against production rather than estimating it.

It came to about 18p per user per month as configured. The interesting part is the breakdown: Supabase was 0.7p of that. Over 85% was observability, dominated by session replay at roughly 15p per user, and two configuration lines accounted for most of the bill. Fixed, the same product costs about 3p per user per month.

That is a six-fold difference in unit economics sitting in two lines of config, and nobody would have found it by reading the code.

[YEMI: worth deciding how much of the cost work goes on the page. My view is all of it: measuring your own unit economics and finding that your database is 4% of your bill is a genuinely uncommon thing for a developer to have done, and it is the section a technical founder would react to. Figures were measured 06/08/2026 and should be labelled as such.]

[YEMI: the metrics on this project (137 users, 203 events, 204 photos, 513 messages) do not match the production figures I measured in August (about 119 users ever, roughly 60 monthly active, 4,369 event rows). One of the two is measuring something different. Tell me which numbers you want to stand and I will make them consistent.]

title: LightLife Church
summary: Live church platform and public website: member management, reporting, QR check-in and media.
body:
LightLife Church runs on this. Not a pitch, not a prototype: a live church platform and public site at lightlifechurch.com, with member management, QR check-in, attendance, programmes, media, giving, forms, voting, a Q&A surface and an admin. 423 commits, sole author.

[YEMI: how did this one come about, and what were they using before? Also worth saying plainly whether this is the same problem as Flock or a different one, because a reader who sees both will ask.]

## The one to talk about is attendance

QR check-in is the feature that sounds trivial and is not. It has to work with a queue of people at a door, on their own phones, on a bad connection, operated by a volunteer who was handed the tablet ninety seconds ago and will not read instructions.

[YEMI: what actually happened the first time this was used live? If something went wrong, that is the best paragraph on this page.]

## Built on my own component library

The interface is Devign, my published component library, with Cloudinary handling media and React Router 7 for routing. That is worth stating for one reason: it is the difference between a design system that exists and a design system that is load-bearing. LightLife is the proof that Devign survives contact with a real deadline.

## Small surfaces that matter more than they look

Short-link redirects, an enquiry flow, testimony submission, a voting surface and a books catalogue are individually unremarkable. Collectively they are most of what a congregation actually touches, and they are the parts that get built last and worst on almost every church site.

[YEMI: pick the one of these you are proudest of and tell me why, and I will expand it into a proper section.]

title: Gr8QM Technovates Platform
summary: 40+ page platform: blog and CMS, courses, job board, certifications and admin dashboards.
body:
Gr8QM Technovates is the company platform: a public site, a blog with its own CMS, courses, a job board, events, certificate verification, invoicing and payment, an admin surface, and the distribution portal for a separate product. Over 40 pages, 370 commits, 359 of them mine, 62 migrations and 10 edge functions.

[YEMI: what was here before, and what was the brief? A platform that grew to forty pages usually replaced something. Saying what, and what was wrong with it, is what turns this from an inventory into a case study.]

## It is not a website, and that is the interesting part

The page list gives it away. Alongside the pages a company site is expected to have, there is `CertificateVerify`, `PayInvoice`, `PaymentSuccess`, `JobDetail`, `EventDetail`, `Glossary`, `Alumni`, `DsgnLaunchpad`, and a full DevignFX portal with its own login, dashboard and download-expiry handling.

Each of those is a small product with its own state and its own failure modes. Certificate verification has to be trustworthy to a stranger who was not the one issued it. Invoicing has to be correct. A download link that has expired has to say so clearly rather than 404.

## One platform carrying several audiences

A prospective student, an alumnus verifying a certificate, a job applicant, someone paying an invoice and a DevignFX customer collecting a build all arrive at the same domain wanting entirely different things. The structural decision was to let them share a shell and a design system while keeping their routes and their data properly separate.

## The honest state of the codebase

There is cruft. `AboutOld`, `HomeOld`, `CareersOld`, `ContactOld`, `PageNotFoundOld` are all still in the tree next to their replacements. That is what iterating on a live company site under time pressure looks like, and leaving the old page in place while the new one is proven is a reasonable thing to do. Not deleting it afterwards is not.

[YEMI: worth deciding whether to say this. I think a short, specific admission like this is worth more than another paragraph of features, because everyone reading has the same files in their own repos. Alternatively I cut it and we clean the files up instead.]

title: OutOut Landing & Deep Links
summary: Landing site with Vercel edge functions serving app-link verification and share previews.
body:
The OutOut landing site, and rather more than a landing site. It serves the app-link verification files that make deep links work on iOS and Android, plus share previews for content inside the app, both through Vercel edge functions. 79 commits, sole author.

## The unglamorous half is the load-bearing half

Universal Links on iOS and App Links on Android both require a file served from the domain at an exact path, with exact content type, no redirect and no caching surprise. Get any of that wrong and links silently open the browser instead of the app. There is no error, no warning and no way for a user to tell you what went wrong beyond "the link does not work".

That is why this is a React site with edge functions rather than a static page: the verification payloads and the share previews both need to be generated and served correctly, per platform, every time.

## Share previews are a growth surface disguised as a technical detail

When someone shares an event from inside the app, what lands in the other person's chat is the entire first impression of the product. A generic card with the app name converts nothing. A card with the actual event, the actual image and the actual time is the difference between a shared link being opened and being ignored, and it has to be rendered server-side because the crawler fetching it does not run JavaScript.

## One domain, two jobs

outout.app is both the marketing site and the infrastructure behind every link the app produces. Keeping those in one codebase is a deliberate trade: slightly more complexity in one place, versus a class of deep-link bug that is almost impossible to diagnose when the two are split.

title: Skoolrithm
summary: Multi-tenant school-management SaaS. Built the Expo/React Native mobile app, live on the App Store, and contributed across the web front-end.
body:
Skoolrithm is a multi-tenant school-management SaaS: a pnpm monorepo with three applications, a tenant web app, a platform admin and an Expo mobile app. I own the mobile app, which is live on the App Store as `com.skoolrithm.app`, and contributed substantially to the other two. I did not own the repository and I am not the founder.

That distinction is worth making plainly, because whole-repository commit counts would have told you I was a minor contributor and that is not true either.

## Why the numbers needed reading properly

By commits across the whole monorepo I look like roughly a third of it. By files touched inside `apps/mobile` I am 416 of 606, about 69%, plus 258 on the tenant app and 100 on the platform.

For a monorepo, per-directory authorship is the real signal. A whole-repo contributor graph can completely hide the fact that one person owns an entire application inside it, in either direction. Mine understated it, and I would rather explain the method than pick the flattering number.

## The mobile app

Expo and React Native, currently v1.0.3, distributed through EAS with over-the-air updates, Firebase for push, and TanStack Query with offline persistence so the app is usable on a school run rather than only on wifi.

[YEMI: what is the single hardest thing you solved in this app? Offline persistence for a school context has some genuinely awkward problems in it (whose data syncs, what a parent sees versus a teacher, what happens when a term rolls over) and one specific war story would carry this whole page.]

## Design lead as well as mobile lead

[YEMI: you are credited as lead designer here as well. What did you actually decide about the design, and did the three applications end up sharing a system or diverging? This is the part that makes it a design engineering case study rather than a mobile one.]

title: WhoDeyGo
summary: Peer-to-peer parcel-carrying marketplace on the London to Lagos corridor.
body:
WhoDeyGo, a peer-to-peer parcel-carrying marketplace on the London to Lagos corridor: travellers with spare luggage allowance matched to people who need something carried. Built in Flutter with Riverpod, go_router and Supabase.

## My role was development, not design

I contributed Flutter development. I did not design this product and I will not take credit for its design. The repository is shared and a meaningful commit count is not mine to claim.

## The corridor is the product

London to Lagos is not an abstract route. It is a specific, high-volume, high-trust-deficit corridor where formal shipping is slow and expensive and informal carrying is already how an enormous amount of goods actually move. The product is not inventing a behaviour, it is trying to make an existing one safer and legible.

## Which makes trust the entire design problem

Two strangers, one of whom is handing over something valuable and one of whom is carrying it through customs. Identity, accountability, what happens when a parcel does not arrive, and what a traveller is and is not agreeing to carry. Almost every hard decision in a product like this is about liability and verification rather than about the matching algorithm.

## Flutter with Riverpod and Drift-style local state

State management matters more than usual here because the app is used in transit: airports, aircraft, foreign networks, roaming turned off. Anything that assumes a live connection at the moment it is needed will fail exactly when the user is most stressed.

title: YarnDok
summary: AI telemedicine interface prioritising medical information hierarchy and accessibility. Live.
body:
YarnDok is an AI telemedicine interface focused on medical information hierarchy and accessibility. Product design, brand, and the front-end build. Now live.

## Medical hierarchy is not an aesthetic problem

A patient reading their own results, or a clinician scanning a summary between appointments, is making a decision with consequences. Getting the order of information wrong does not make the screen uglier, it makes the wrong thing the first thing read. That is a different design standard to almost anything else in this portfolio.

The working rule was that severity and actionability outrank recency and completeness. What do I need to do, and how urgently, comes before the full record.

## Accessibility here is not a compliance checkbox

The population using a telemedicine product skews towards people who are unwell, older, anxious, on a phone in poor light, or all four at once. Contrast, target size, and language that does not require a clinical vocabulary are not accommodations for a minority. They are the median case.

## AI in a clinical context has to be legible about its own uncertainty

An interface that presents a model's suggestion with the same confidence as a lab value is dangerous. The design work is mostly about making the boundary visible: what is measured, what is inferred, and what a human still has to decide. A confident-looking answer is the failure mode.

## Design through to code

I took this one from research and identity through to the front end rather than handing a prototype over. For an interface this dependent on hierarchy and contrast that matters, because the gap between an approved comp and a built screen is exactly where careful spacing and type decisions usually get lost.

title: HUM
summary: React Native mobile app, in TestFlight beta.
body:
HUM is a React Native mobile app built with Expo and Supabase, currently in TestFlight beta. Supporting contributor.

## The honest scope

This is not my app. I contributed to it as part of the wider AIENAI portfolio and I do not have commits in the repository, so the credit is supporting contributor. It is here because it is real, shipped work I touched, and leaving it off would make the portfolio less accurate rather than more impressive.

## Shipping to the App Store is the part that is not glamorous

Review, provisioning, build signing, and the fact that a mistake costs days rather than a redeploy. Web work has conditioned a generation of engineers to treat release as free. Mobile does not let you, and the discipline it forces back into a team (finish it, test it, then ship it) is usually good for the web work as well.

## Expo, and what it buys

Expo with EAS handles the build and update machinery that otherwise eats a week per platform, and over-the-air updates mean a copy fix does not need a review cycle. It is the same trade as any framework: less control, far less time spent on the parts nobody sees.
